title: Respiratory syncytial virus-induced ADAM17 activity controls maintenance of epithelial barrier integrity and promotes syncytium formation

analysis.research_question_and_background: RSV infection causes epithelial injury, barrier disruption, and syncytium formation, but the regulatory host defense mechanisms involved remain poorly defined.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study investigated RSV-induced ADAM17 activity in human lung tissue, demonstrating its role in promoting syncytium formation and viral spread while controlling epithelial barrier integrity.
analysis.methods: The study used genetic loss and pharmacological inhibition of ADAM17 to assess its effects on RSV-induced syncytium formation, post-entry viral spread, and viral titers.
analysis.main_results: Genetic loss or pharmacological inhibition of ADAM17 reduced RSV-induced formation of syncytia, post-entry viral spread, and viral titers.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings identify ADAM17 as a host factor that supports viral dissemination, highlighting its dual role in RSV infection.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings suggest that ADAM17 activity represents a biological trade-off between viral dissemination and tissue protection, which may inform future therapeutic strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study provides moderate confidence by demonstrating functional effects of ADAM17 inhibition in RSV infection, but it does not address broader clinical implications or long-term outcomes.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the role of ADAM17 in respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection, revealing that RSV-induced ADAM17 activity promotes syncytium formation and viral spread while maintaining epithelial barrier integrity. The research demonstrates that genetic or pharmacological inhibition of ADAM17 reduces viral dissemination but may compromise epithelial defenses. These findings highlight a dual role for ADAM17 in RSV infection, balancing viral propagation with tissue protection. The study provides moderate confidence in its conclusions, as it focuses on functional effects in a controlled setting without addressing broader clinical implications. The results suggest that targeting ADAM17 for antiviral therapy may present challenges due to its essential role in preserving epithelial integrity. This work identifies ADAM17 as a key host factor in RSV pathogenesis and underscores the need for further research into its therapeutic potential and limitations.

title: Molecular detection of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in hospitalized children at the University Hospital Center of Brazzaville, Republic of the Congo

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory viral infections are among the most common diseases responsible for morbidity and mortality among children in sub-Saharan Africa, with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) being a major contributor.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The objective of this study was to detect RSV among hospitalized children under five years of age with acute respiratory infections at the University Hospital Center of Brazzaville in the Republic of the Congo. A total of 81 nasopharyngeal swab samples were collected from children aged ≤5 years who were admitted to the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit and Neonatology Department of the University Hospital Center of Brazzaville with acute respiratory infections between August and December 2023.
analysis.methods: Respiratory viruses were identified using rapid antigen detection assays and reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR).
analysis.main_results: Rapid antigen tests detected SARS-CoV-2 in 2 cases (2.5%), whereas RSV and influenza A and B were not detected. In contrast, RT-qPCR identified RSV in 4 samples (4.9%).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These findings confirm the circulation of RSV among hospitalized children at the University Hospital Center of Brazzaville and highlight the superior sensitivity of RT-qPCR over rapid antigen tests for RSV detection.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the importance of using RT-qPCR for accurate RSV detection in clinical settings, which can inform improved diagnostic strategies and surveillance in sub-Saharan Africa.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was limited by its focus on hospitalized children and the use of a single diagnostic method, but the evidence is strong as it directly reports RSV detection using RT-qPCR in a specific population and setting.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to detect respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in hospitalized children under five years of age with acute respiratory infections at the University Hospital Center of Brazzaville, Republic of the Congo. A total of 81 nasopharyngeal swab samples were collected between August and December 2023. Rapid antigen detection assays identified SARS-CoV-2 in 2 cases (2.5%), but RSV and influenza A and B were not detected. In contrast, RT-qPCR identified RSV in 4 samples (4.9%). All RSV-positive patients were male, aged over 28 days, and hospitalized in the pediatric intensive care unit. The main clinical signs observed were respiratory distress (100%), cough (75%), fever (50%) and rhinorrhea (50%). These findings confirm the circulation of RSV in this setting and highlight the superior sensitivity of RT-qPCR over rapid antigen tests for RSV detection. The study provides important insights into the diagnostic challenges of RSV in sub-Saharan Africa and underscores the need for more sensitive testing methods in clinical practice.

title: Development and Validation of machine learning models for early prediction of severe Respiratory Syncytial Virus pneumonia in children

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) is a leading cause of severe respiratory infections, particularly pneumonia, in children, especially those under the age of five. The incidence of severe RSV pneumonia has risen in recent years, underscoring the need for an effective predictive tool.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective analysis was conducted involving 180 children with confirmed RSV pneumonia, categorized into severe (n = 62) and non-severe (n = 118) groups. Clinical, laboratory, and imaging data were collected at admission.
analysis.methods: Features selection was performed using LASSO regression and the Boruta algorithm. Subsequently, eight machine learning models were developed, including Logistic Regression, Multilayer Perceptron, Support Vector Machine, Decision Tree, Random Forest (RF), AdaBoost, and Extreme Gradient Boosting. Model performance was evaluated using standard metrics, such as area under the curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and F1 score.
analysis.main_results: Seven features were identified for model development. Among the models, RF exhibited the best performance, with an AUC of 0.853, sensitivity of 0.895, specificity of 0.714, accuracy of 0.778, and F1-score of 0.739 in the testing cohort. DCA demonstrated that the RF model provided a significant net benefit, indicating its clinical utility for early intervention. SHAP analysis revealed that respiratory rate and shortness of breath were the most influential features in predicting severe RSV pneumonia.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The RF model demonstrated strong predictive performance for identifying severe RSV pneumonia in children, providing a novel approach for early detection and timely intervention.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the development of early surveillance systems and guide timely clinical interventions for children at risk of severe RSV pneumonia.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and potential for selection bias. However, the model's performance metrics suggest moderate evidence for its clinical utility in predicting severe RSV pneumonia.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to develop and validate machine learning models for early prediction of severe Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) pneumonia in children. A retrospective analysis of 180 children with confirmed RSV pneumonia, divided into severe and non-severe groups, was conducted. Clinical, laboratory, and imaging data were collected at admission, and features were selected using LASSO regression and the Boruta algorithm. Eight machine learning models were developed, with Random Forest (RF) showing the best performance, achieving an AUC of 0.853, sensitivity of 0.895, specificity of 0.714, accuracy of 0.778, and F1-score of 0.739. Decision Curve Analysis (DCA) indicated the RF model's clinical utility for early intervention, while SHAP analysis highlighted respiratory rate and shortness of breath as the most influential features. The authors concluded that the RF model provides a novel approach for early detection of severe RSV pneumonia, which could inform surveillance and intervention strategies. The study's retrospective design and potential for selection bias limit its evidence strength, though the results suggest moderate confidence in the model's utility.

title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV)–An Urgent Priority in Respiratory Disease Prevention

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of lower respiratory tract disease in infants, young children, older adults, and individuals with cardiopulmonary comorbidities or immunocompromised states.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This editorial synthesizes current evidence and policy directions to underscore priority populations and outline actionable levers in financing, procurement, and integrated maternal–child health delivery to accelerate access to RSV prevention.
analysis.methods: Recent advances enable layered prevention through maternal vaccination for infant protection, long-acting monoclonal antibodies for newborns and select toddlers, and vaccines for older adults.
analysis.main_results: This editorial underscores priority populations, synthesizes current evidence and policy directions, and outlines actionable levers in financing, procurement, and integrated maternal–child health delivery to accelerate access, making RSV prevention an urgent and achievable global health priority.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The editorial highlights the potential for RSV prevention to become an urgent and achievable global health priority through targeted interventions and improved access.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the need for improved surveillance, equitable access to prevention strategies, and integrated delivery systems to address RSV-related health disparities.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report specific limitations, but the editorial is based on a synthesis of current evidence and policy directions, which provides a moderate level of confidence.

analysis.summary_en: This editorial emphasizes the urgent need for RSV prevention as a global health priority, highlighting its significant role in causing lower respiratory tract disease across various vulnerable populations. It outlines recent advances in prevention strategies, including maternal vaccination, monoclonal antibodies, and vaccines for older adults, and stresses the importance of addressing inequities in surveillance, affordability, and delivery, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. The editorial calls for actionable measures in financing, procurement, and integrated maternal–child health systems to improve access. While the evidence is based on a synthesis of current data and policy directions, it does not report specific limitations, resulting in a moderate confidence assessment. These findings have important implications for public health, underscoring the need for targeted interventions and equitable distribution of prevention tools.

title: Integrin-FAK signaling dependent non-canonical ISGylation by extracellular ISG15 restricts human respiratory syncytial virus infection in epithelial cells

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the role of extracellular ISG15 in antiviral activity during human respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection and whether it could activate IFN-independent ISGylation through alternative cellular signaling pathways.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used IFN and IFN signaling incompetent epithelial cells infected with human respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) or treated with purified human ISG15 protein. Additional studies were conducted with IFN competent cells treated with IFN signaling inhibitors, along with extracellular ISG15 blocking antibody and immunofluorescence analysis.
analysis.methods: The methods included using integrin-FAK pathway inhibitors and mutant ISG15 protein generated based on in silico modeling that failed to interact with integrin. A protein chase experiment was performed with protein synthesis inhibitor treated cells to demonstrate post-translational regulation.
analysis.main_results: The study identified an alternative non-canonical ISGylation route initiated by extracellular ISG15 and mediated by integrin-FAK signaling, in contrast to the classical IFN-driven ISGylation. It also showed that extracellular ISG15 enhances the post-translational stability of basal intracellular ISG15 protein to support ISGylation in the absence of ISG15 transcriptional upregulation.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted these findings as evidence of extracellular ISG15 acting as a soluble antiviral factor that triggers IFN-independent ISGylation and restricts virus infection in epithelial cells. This represents a novel mechanism of antiviral immunity involving integrin-FAK signaling.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings have broad implications for antiviral immunity, disease resolution, and the development of host-directed therapeutic strategies for various diseases, including respiratory syncytial virus infection.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's evidence is based on in vitro experiments using IFN signaling incompetent cells and inhibitors, which may limit generalizability to in vivo settings. The evidence strength is moderate due to the reliance on cell culture models and the absence of clinical data.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the role of extracellular ISG15 in antiviral activity during human respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection. It identifies an alternative non-canonical ISGylation route initiated by extracellular ISG15 and mediated by integrin-FAK signaling, independent of IFN. The findings demonstrate that extracellular ISG15 acts as a soluble antiviral factor, enhancing post-translational stability of intracellular ISG15 protein to support ISGylation. This mechanism has implications for antiviral immunity and the development of host-directed therapies. The study uses in vitro models, which may limit generalizability to in vivo settings, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

title: Maternal vaccination against COVID-19, influenza, pertussis, and respiratory syncytial virus: a scoping review

analysis.scope_and_question: Pregnancy and early infancy are periods of heightened vulnerability, with SARS-CoV-2 and influenza infections potentially linked to adverse pregnancy outcomes, including preterm birth and stillbirth.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A comprehensive literature search across multiple databases of studies published from January 2000 to October 2025 identified 635 publications (540 publications of primary studies, 95 evidence syntheses). Studies on COVID-19 (260 publications of studies, 45 reviews), influenza (161 publications of studies, 29 reviews), pertussis (113 publications of studies, 20 reviews), and RSV (20 publications of studies, 11 reviews) were analysed.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Maternal vaccination provides direct protection to mothers by active immunisation and to infants by passive immunisation. Available evidence on COVID-19, influenza, and pertussis vaccination on efficacy, effectiveness, safety and immunogenicity outcomes is considerable.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: It includes information on the outcome domains studied and if timing of vaccination was examined, with the aim of identifying evidence gaps and supporting decision-makers in choosing priority areas for subsequent systematic review topics. RSV vaccination evidence is limited. Updated systematic reviews would be helpful to clarify the optimal timing of COVID-19 and influenza vaccination and the effectiveness and safety of the coadministration of influenza and pertussis vaccines.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: This scoping review mapped and described published literature on maternal vaccination against COVID-19, influenza, pertussis, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).

analysis.summary_en: This scoping review focuses on maternal vaccination against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), alongside other pathogens such as SARS-CoV-2, influenza, and pertussis. It highlights the importance of maternal vaccination in protecting both mothers and infants through active and passive immunisation. The review identified 635 publications, including 20 studies and 11 reviews on RSV, and found that evidence on RSV vaccination is limited. While substantial evidence exists for the efficacy, effectiveness, safety, and immunogenicity of vaccines against other pathogens, the review underscores the need for updated systematic reviews to address gaps in understanding the optimal timing of vaccination and the safety of coadministration of vaccines. The findings aim to support decision-makers in prioritizing areas for further research and policy development.

title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccination Strongly Induces RSVpreF-specific IgG and Neutralizing Activity in Immunocompromised Individuals.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess the immunogenicity of RSVpreF vaccines in immunocompromised individuals, addressing the need for optimized vaccination strategies in transplant recipients and patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and hemodialysis. Previous studies had shown promising CD4 T-cell responses and IgG antibodies but lacked data on functional humoral responses and associations between cellular and humoral endpoints.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study evaluated RSVpreF-specific IgG and neutralizing activity in 61 CKD patients, 15 hemodialysis patients, 46 kidney transplant recipients, and 31 lung transplant recipients, using ELISA and a pseudovirus assay.
analysis.methods: RSVpreF-specific IgG was measured by ELISA, and neutralizing activity was assessed using an RSV-pseudovirus assay. Comprehensive correlation analyses were performed to assess associations between vaccine-induced humoral immune parameters and cellular immunity.
analysis.main_results: RSV vaccination induced robust functional humoral immunity in all tested immunocompromised patient groups, with the lowest responses observed in kidney transplant recipients. Correlations with CD4 T-cell responses were less pronounced.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study demonstrated that RSV vaccination induces strong functional humoral immunity in various immunocompromised populations, highlighting the need for tailored vaccination strategies in kidney transplant recipients and patients on mycophenolate mofetil/methylprednisolone (MMF/MPA).
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that RSV vaccination can be effective in immunocompromised individuals, but strategies may need to be optimized for kidney transplant recipients to ensure adequate protection. This has implications for surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment of RSV infection in these patient groups.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the small sample sizes and the focus on a single vaccine formulation, which may limit generalizability. The evidence strength is moderate due to the observational nature of the study and the need for further research to confirm these findings.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the immunogenicity of RSVpreF vaccines in immunocompromised individuals, including CKD, hemodialysis, kidney transplant, and lung transplant recipients. It demonstrated robust functional humoral immunity in all groups, with the lowest responses in kidney transplant recipients, highlighting the need for tailored vaccination strategies.

title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection and Cardiovascular Diseases in Adults: Disease Burden, Cardiac Complications, Pathophysiology, and Prevention Strategies

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection is increasingly recognized as a significant cause of morbidity, hospitalization, and mortality in adults, particularly those with pre-existing cardiovascular diseases. The study aimed to explore the relationship between RSV infection and cardiovascular complications in adults.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a comprehensive review of observational studies and systematic analyses published in recent years, focusing on hospitalized adults with RSV infection, especially those with pre-existing cardiovascular conditions.
analysis.methods: The analysis synthesized findings from observational studies and systematic reviews, emphasizing the mechanisms linking RSV infection to cardiovascular complications and the potential impact of vaccination strategies on these outcomes.
analysis.main_results: Recent studies have shown that approximately 20% of hospitalized adults with RSV infection experience acute cardiac events, with acute heart failure being the most frequently reported complication. Individuals with pre-existing heart failure have a significantly increased risk of cardiac complications following RSV infection.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that RSV infection can trigger acute cardiovascular events, highlighting the need for targeted prevention strategies in high-risk populations. This study provides novel insights into the bidirectional relationship between RSV and cardiovascular diseases.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings underscore the importance of RSV vaccination in adults with cardiovascular diseases to reduce the risk of severe complications and hospitalizations, offering a basis for future public health interventions.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is based on observational studies and systematic reviews, which may be subject to biases and confounding factors. However, the high prevalence of cardiac complications in RSV-infected adults with pre-existing conditions supports a moderate confidence in the findings.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the relationship between respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection and cardiovascular complications in adults, highlighting that RSV is a growing cause of morbidity, hospitalization, and mortality in this population. It identifies acute heart failure as the most common cardiac complication, particularly in individuals with pre-existing heart failure. The authors emphasize the bidirectional interaction between RSV and cardiovascular diseases, suggesting that targeted prevention strategies, such as vaccination, are crucial for high-risk groups. While the evidence is based on observational studies and systematic reviews, the moderate confidence in findings is supported by the high prevalence of cardiac events in RSV-infected adults with underlying conditions. The study calls for further research to explore the specific cardiovascular outcomes associated with RSV vaccination.

title: Morbidity and mortality of respiratory syncytial virus versus influenza virus infections in hospitalized older adults: an adjusted comparative analysis

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to compare the morbidity and mortality of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections with influenza virus infections in hospitalized older adults. The background highlighted the importance of understanding the clinical impact of these viral infections in this vulnerable population.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was an adjusted comparative analysis conducted in hospitalized older adults. It focused on respiratory syncytial virus and influenza virus infections, comparing their associated morbidity and mortality outcomes.
analysis.methods: The methods involved analyzing data from hospitalized older adults to compare the clinical outcomes of respiratory syncytial virus and influenza virus infections. The analysis included adjustments for confounding factors to ensure accurate comparison.
analysis.main_results: The study directly observed that respiratory syncytial virus infections were associated with higher morbidity and mortality compared to influenza virus infections in hospitalized older adults.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted these findings as highlighting the greater severity of RSV infections in older adults, which is a novel insight into the differential impact of these viruses on hospitalization outcomes.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings can inform targeted surveillance and management strategies for respiratory syncytial virus in older adults, potentially improving clinical outcomes and resource allocation.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's evidence is limited by its observational nature and potential confounding factors, resulting in a moderate confidence assessment.

analysis.summary_en: This study compares the morbidity and mortality of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and influenza virus infections in hospitalized older adults. It highlights the greater clinical impact of RSV, suggesting a need for targeted surveillance and management. The analysis is observational and adjusted for confounding factors, leading to a moderate confidence assessment. The findings may inform public health strategies for older adult populations, emphasizing the importance of distinguishing between these viral infections in clinical settings.

title: Epidemiology and lagged climatic drivers of pediatric viral lower respiratory tract infections in Tianjin, China (2023–2025)

analysis.research_question_and_background: Following the lifting of pandemic-era restrictions, China experienced a sharp resurgence in pediatric respiratory infections; however, post-pandemic epidemiological and climatic data on lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) from the temperate continental climate of northern China remain scarce.
analysis.study_design_and_population: In this retrospective, single-center surveillance study, we characterized the post-pandemic epidemiology of six respiratory viruses in children hospitalized with LRTI in Tianjin and assessed their pathogen-specific, lagged climatic associations.
analysis.methods: Children aged 0–18 years hospitalized between January 2023 and December 2025 were tested by targeted next-generation sequencing for human rhinovirus (HRV), adenovirus (ADV), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), human bocavirus (HBoV), influenza virus (IFV), and human metapneumovirus (HMPV).
analysis.main_results: Among 2,597 virus-positive cases, the leading pathogens were HRV (30.7%), ADV (26.6%), and RSV (20.6%), followed by HBoV (12.1%), IFV (6.0%), and HMPV (4.0%).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Age distributions differed by pathogen (p<0.05): RSV and HBoV predominated in infants and toddlers, HRV and HMPV in preschoolers, ADV in school-aged children, and IFV across the older preschool-to-school-age range; males predominated for all viruses except IFV.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The summer peak of HBoV and the seasonally independent climatic drivers of RSV and HMPV provide a preliminary basis that, if confirmed with higher-resolution data, could inform pathogen-tailored, climate-informed surveillance in northern Chinese megacities.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: After adjustment for seasonality and secular trend, the unadjusted associations of IFV with humidity and temperature disappeared, indicating that they largely reflected shared seasonality.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the post-pandemic epidemiology and climatic drivers of pediatric viral lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) in Tianjin, China, focusing on respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). The research highlights the distinct age-specific and seasonal patterns of RSV, with a notable predominance in infants and toddlers. The study employed a retrospective, single-center surveillance approach using targeted next-generation sequencing to identify viral pathogens and assess their associations with climatic factors. Key findings include RSV's unique climatic associations with temperature and wind speed at a 1-month lag, which suggest potential for climate-informed surveillance strategies. However, the study acknowledges limitations, such as the influence of shared seasonality on some results, and emphasizes the need for higher-resolution data to confirm these findings. The results contribute to understanding the dynamics of RSV in northern China and may inform targeted public health interventions.

title: Position statement of the Mexican Academy of Pediatrics regarding strategies to prevent respiratory syncytial virus infection in MexicoÓ?s pediatric population

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is one of the leading causes of acute lower respiratory tract infection, bronchiolitis, pneumonia, and hospitalization among infants and young children, with the highest risk of severe disease observed in infants younger than six months, preterm infants, and children with bronchopulmonary dysplasia, congenital heart disease, immunocompromising conditions, and other underlying comorbidities.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This position statement from the Mexican Academy of Pediatrics reviews the epidemiological, clinical, and real-world effectiveness evidence regarding currently available strategies for the prevention of RSV infection in the pediatric population.
analysis.methods: Maternal vaccination between 32 and 36 weeks of gestation promotes transplacental antibody transfer and provides protection to infants during the first months of life.
analysis.main_results: Monoclonal antibodies, particularly nirsevimab, have demonstrated significant reductions in lower respiratory tract infection, hospitalization, intensive care unit admission, and severe RSV-associated disease, with a favorable safety profile.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: In recent years, the development of novel preventive strategies has transformed the approach to RSV prevention, particularly through maternal immunization with a bivalent prefusion F protein vaccine and passive immunoprophylaxis with long-acting monoclonal antibodies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Based on disease burden, national seasonality, availability of preventive products, and the characteristics of the Mexican health care system, the Mexican Academy of Pediatrics proposes a complementary and progressive strategy integrating maternal vaccination and monoclonal antibody immunoprophylaxis, initially prioritizing high-risk infants and gradually expanding coverage to all susceptible infants.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Implementation should consider efficacy, safety, cost-effectiveness, operational feasibility, equity, and timely access.

analysis.summary_en: This position statement from the Mexican Academy of Pediatrics addresses the need for effective strategies to prevent respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection in the pediatric population, emphasizing the significant clinical burden and seasonal circulation of RSV in Mexico. The study reviews the epidemiological, clinical, and real-world effectiveness of current preventive measures, including maternal immunization with a bivalent prefusion F protein vaccine and passive immunoprophylaxis with monoclonal antibodies like nirsevimab. The findings indicate that monoclonal antibodies have shown substantial reductions in RSV-related hospitalizations and severe disease with a favorable safety profile. The authors interpret these results as a transformative shift in RSV prevention, advocating for a complementary and progressive strategy that prioritizes high-risk infants and expands coverage to all susceptible infants. The proposed strategy considers factors such as efficacy, safety, cost-effectiveness, and equitable access. The evidence is strong and grounded in the Mexican health care system's context, but the implementation requires careful evaluation of these factors to ensure operational feasibility and public health impact.

title: Comorbidity-associated reduction in humoral and cellular immunity to respiratory syncytial virus in older adults at a tertiary care setting in India

analysis.research_question_and_background: Older adults with comorbidities experience substantial morbidity from respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), yet evidence from low- and middle-income countries on functional RSV immunity, particularly the relationship between humoral and cellular immune responses remain limited.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We conducted a cross-sectional study among adults aged ≥ 60 years at a tertiary care center in New Delhi, India. Individuals attending outpatient clinics or admitted for non-acute, non-respiratory conditions were eligible. Enrolled individuals were found to be RSV seropositive in all age groups.
analysis.methods: We conducted a cross-sectional sero-immunologic study between January and December 2024 at a tertiary care center in New Delhi, India. Majority of the samples from older adults failed to produce IL-2, IFN-γ or TNF-α in CD4+/CD8+ cells upon stimulation with RSV peptide pool.
analysis.main_results: The magnitude of neutralizing antibody titers was lower in older adults with comorbidities compared to young healthy adults and we found a positive correlation between binding IgG and neutralizing antibody titers. Neutralizing activity was significantly lower in older adults with chronic liver disease (p = 0·009) and malignancy (p = 0·04). RSV-specific T-cell responses were significantly lower in older adults than in healthy young adults, with median IFN-γ ELISpot values of 8 and 68 spot-forming units (SFU) per million cells, respectively (p = 0·0068).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that comorbidities in older adults are associated with reduced functional RSV immunity, which may explain their increased susceptibility to severe RSV disease.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform targeted surveillance and interventions for RSV in older adults with comorbidities, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where such data are scarce.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its cross-sectional design, which does not establish causality. The evidence is moderate as it is based on observational data and does not include longitudinal follow-up.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the impact of comorbidities on functional RSV immunity in older adults at a tertiary care center in New Delhi, India. It finds that older adults with comorbidities have lower neutralizing antibody titers and RSV-specific T-cell responses compared to young healthy adults. The results suggest that comorbidities may reduce immune function against RSV, potentially increasing vulnerability to severe disease. The study is cross-sectional, limiting causal inference, and provides moderate evidence due to its observational nature. These findings have implications for understanding immune dynamics in RSV infection among older adults and could guide future research and public health strategies in low- and middle-income countries.

title: Rapid subtype-specific detection of respiratory syncytial virus A and B using an RNase HII-dependent RT-LAMP lateral flow assay

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to develop a rapid, accurate, and subtype-specific point-of-care diagnostic platform for respiratory syncytial virus A (RSV A) and B (RSV B) to improve POC diagnostics and epidemiological surveillance. The research addressed the need for simultaneous detection and subtype discrimination of RSV A and B, which is crucial for effective management and surveillance of respiratory infections.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was conducted using a retrospective panel of 281 archived nasopharyngeal swab specimens from Korea University Guro Hospital, Seoul, Republic of Korea. The specimens were tested for RSV positivity, negativity, and subtype classification using the AllplexTM Respiratory Panel 1 assay as the reference method.
analysis.methods: The RSV A/B rh-RT-LAMP-NALF assay was developed using RNase HII-dependent RT-LAMP combined with NALF detection. The assay was evaluated for sensitivity, specificity, and cross-reactivity using clinical specimen dilution series and a panel of 281 archived nasopharyngeal swab specimens. Comparative RT-PCR and rapid antigen detection tests were also performed for performance evaluation.
analysis.main_results: The RSV A/B rh-RT-LAMP-NALF assay demonstrated sensitivities of 95.4% (95% CI: 88.8%–98.2%) for RSV A and 97.9% (95% CI: 92.6%–99.4%) for RSV B, with no false-positive results observed in the 100 RSV-negative specimens. The assay showed comparable performance to the AllplexTM SARS-CoV-2/FluA/FluB/RSV assay and higher sensitivity than the STANDARD Q RSV Ag Test.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the results as demonstrating the RSV A/B rh-RT-LAMP-NALF assay's high sensitivity and specificity, making it a valuable tool for rapid and accurate POC diagnostics and surveillance of RSV A and B.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that the RSV A/B rh-RT-LAMP-NALF assay can improve the detection and surveillance of RSV A and B, aiding in the management and control of respiratory syncytial virus infections.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the use of a single reference method and the lack of longitudinal data. The evidence strength is moderate due to the retrospective nature of the study and the absence of a randomized controlled trial.

analysis.summary_en: This study developed and validated a rapid, accurate, and subtype-specific RT-LAMP-NALF assay for detecting RSV A and B from nasopharyngeal swab specimens. The assay showed high sensitivity and specificity, comparable to RT-PCR and higher than antigen-based tests, making it a valuable tool for POC diagnostics and surveillance.

title: Postpandemic Trends in Pediatric Respiratory Virus Hospitalizations: A Multicenter Study, 2019-2025.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand postpandemic trends in pediatric respiratory virus hospitalizations, particularly focusing on how the epidemiology of acute lower respiratory tract infections changed in children following the COVID-19 pandemic.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective multicenter study was conducted across 16 pediatric hospitals in Italy, analyzing hospitalizations of children younger than 18 years with RSV, influenza, adenovirus, parainfluenza virus, rhinovirus infection, or bronchiolitis of unspecified viral etiology from January 2019 to March 2025.
analysis.methods: Temporal trends were assessed across six consecutive seasons using ICD-9-CM diagnostic codes to identify hospitalizations and annual and monthly hospitalization rates per 100,000 children were calculated using national demographic data.
analysis.main_results: Overall, 23,981 hospitalizations were recorded. RSV was the most frequent pathogen (42.5%), followed by influenza (18.6%), adenovirus (9.9%), and rhinovirus (7.3%). Hospitalizations declined sharply in 2020 and subsequently increased, peaking in 2024 (n = 4903; +30.8% vs. During the 2024–2025 season, total admissions decreased by 17.2% compared with 2023–2024 (3390 vs. 4095), mainly due to a marked reduction in RSV-related hospitalizations (−41.6%, 1230 vs. 2107), with modest increases in influenza-, adenovirus-, and rhinovirus-associated admissions.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as highlighting changing pathogen-specific patterns in pediatric hospitalizations post-pandemic and emphasized the need for continued viral surveillance.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the need for ongoing viral surveillance and highlight the importance of monitoring pathogen-specific trends to guide public health interventions and resource allocation.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and reliance on ICD-9-CM codes, which may introduce some bias. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the observational nature of the study.

analysis.summary_en: This multicenter study analyzed postpandemic trends in pediatric respiratory virus hospitalizations in Italy from 2019 to 2025. It found that respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) was the most frequent pathogen, followed by influenza, adenovirus, and rhinovirus. Hospitalizations declined sharply in 2020, then increased, peaking in 2024, and subsequently decreased again in 2024–2025, primarily due to a significant reduction in RSV-related admissions. The study highlights changing pathogen-specific patterns and underscores the importance of continued viral surveillance. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the observational design and potential coding biases.

title: From Selective Prophylaxis to Broad Infant RSV Protection: A Bibliometric Analysis and Evidence Gap Map, 1998–2025

analysis.research_question_and_background: Infant respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) prevention has moved from selective palivizumab prophylaxis toward broader protection through long-acting monoclonal antibodies and maternal vaccination. The study aimed to examine how this research area evolved and whether original studies address evidence needed for implementation at scale.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study conducted a bibliometric analysis and evidence-gap mapping study of Web of Science Core Collection records from 1998 to 2025. The bibliometric corpus included 2004 publications; 1581 original articles underwent relevance screening and targeted audit, yielding 1227 studies for evidence-gap mapping.
analysis.methods: The study used a bibliometric analysis and evidence-gap mapping approach to evaluate the evolution of research on infant RSV prevention. A random sample of 150 articles was used to validate relevance screening.
analysis.main_results: Publication output rose sharply after 2022, with 2023−2025 accounting for 35.0% of the bibliometric corpus. Validation showed 86.7% agreement (Cohen's kappa = 0.52).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The literature has shifted toward broad infant RSV protection, but implementation-relevant evidence remains uneven. Earlier work centered on palivizumab, preterm infants, and hospitalization; recent studies increasingly addressed nirsevimab, maternal RSV vaccination, implementation, and vaccine candidates.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the need for comparative and program-level research to determine how maternal vaccination and infant monoclonal antibody strategies can be implemented and coordinated across health systems while minimizing missed opportunities for protection.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on abstract-only data, which may not capture detailed findings. The evidence strength is moderate, as the study provides a broad overview of trends but does not include specific results or detailed analyses.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the evolution of research on infant respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) prevention from selective palivizumab prophylaxis to broader strategies involving monoclonal antibodies and maternal vaccination. A bibliometric analysis and evidence-gap mapping of 2004 publications from 1998 to 2025 revealed a sharp increase in publication output after 2022, with 35.0% of the corpus published in 2023−2025. Validation of relevance screening showed 86.7% agreement. The literature has shifted toward broad infant RSV protection, but implementation-relevant evidence remains uneven. Earlier work focused on palivizumab, preterm infants, and hospitalization, while recent studies increasingly address nirsevimab, maternal RSV vaccination, and vaccine candidates. The findings highlight the need for comparative and program-level research to coordinate maternal vaccination and infant monoclonal antibody strategies across health systems. The study is limited by its abstract-only data and moderate evidence strength.

title: Nirsevimab in the New Era of RSV Prevention: Current Evidence, Emerging Challenges, and Future Perspectives

analysis.scope_and_question: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the leading cause of lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) and hospitalization in infants and young children worldwide, with the highest disease burden occurring in otherwise healthy term infants during the first 6 months of life.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: Evidence from randomized clinical trials and large real-world studies consistently demonstrates that a single dose of Nirsevimab provides season-long protection against RSV-associated LRTI and reduces hospitalization rate across diverse infant populations, while maintaining an excellent safety profile.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Current evidence supports Nirsevimab as a major advance in infant RSV prevention.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Emerging data also support its effectiveness in routine clinical practice, although important uncertainties remain regarding long-term epidemiological effects, viral evolution, resistance, comparative effectiveness with maternal immunization, and optimal implementation across different healthcare settings.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: However, continued surveillance, comparative effectiveness studies, and equitable global implementation will be essential to maximize its long-term public health impact.

analysis.summary_en: This review focuses on the role of Nirsevimab in preventing severe respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) disease in infants. It highlights that RSV is the leading cause of lower respiratory tract infections and hospitalizations in young children, particularly in otherwise healthy term infants during their first six months. The evidence base includes randomized clinical trials and real-world studies, which show that Nirsevimab provides season-long protection against RSV-associated LRTI and reduces hospitalization rates with a favorable safety profile. While current data support Nirsevimab as a significant advancement in RSV prevention, uncertainties remain about its long-term epidemiological effects, viral evolution, resistance, and comparative effectiveness with maternal immunization. The review emphasizes the need for ongoing surveillance, comparative studies, and equitable global implementation to optimize its public health impact.

title: SRGAP2‐AS1 Regulates RSV Replication and EMT‐Associated Changes Through PTBP1 and ZEB1

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of lower respiratory tract disease, but the contribution of long non‐coding RNAs (lncRNAs) to RSV‐induced epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT)‐associated changes remains unclear.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We used transcriptomic screening in RSV‐exposed BEAS‐2B cells to identify candidate lncRNAs and then examined SRGAP2‐AS1 in cell and mouse models.
analysis.methods: Expression was measured by RT‐qPCR, and loss‐ and gain‐of‐function experiments were combined with RNA immunoprecipitation, co‐immunoprecipitation, Western blot analysis, and TCID 50 assays.
analysis.main_results: SRGAP2‐AS1 was increased in RSV‐infected BEAS‐2B cells and mouse lung tissue. Silencing SRGAP2‐AS1 reduced viral replication, lowered IL‐6 and IL‐1β mRNA, increased IFN‐β mRNA, and attenuated EMT‐associated marker changes in RSV‐infected BEAS‐2B cells.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These findings support regulatory relationships among SRGAP2‐AS1, PTBP1, and ZEB1 during RSV infection.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings may inform future studies on the role of lncRNAs in RSV pathogenesis and suggest potential targets for therapeutic intervention.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The causal order of the viral and immune‐related changes, and the in vivo relevance of the EMT‐associated phenotype, remain unresolved.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the role of SRGAP2‐AS1 in RSV infection, focusing on its regulation of viral replication and EMT-associated changes. The research highlights the involvement of SRGAP2‐AS1 in modulating immune responses and epithelial markers through interactions with PTBP1 and ZEB1. The findings suggest a regulatory network involving these molecules during RSV infection, which could provide insights into potential therapeutic targets. However, the causal order of these interactions and their in vivo relevance remain unclear, indicating limitations in the current evidence. The study contributes to understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying RSV-induced EMT and offers a foundation for further research into lncRNA functions in viral pathogenesis.

title: Surveillance for severe influenza, COVID-19, and RSV in patients admitted to sentinel Australian hospitals in 2025: the Influenza Complications Alert Network (FluCAN) and the Paediatric Active Enhanced Disease Surveillance (PAEDS) system

analysis.research_question_and_background: Influenza, coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are common acute respiratory infections and are a cause of significant morbidity and mortality.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The Influenza Complications Alert Network (FluCAN) and the Paediatric Active Enhanced Disease Surveillance (PAEDS) are collaborative sentinel hospital-based surveillance programs that operate at 23 sites across all jurisdictions in Australia. Influenza, COVID-19 and RSV patients were defined as those hospitalised due to an acute respiratory infection at the sentinel hospitals with virus confirmation by nucleic acid detection.
analysis.methods: The study used a sentinel surveillance system to monitor hospitalisations with laboratory-confirmed influenza, COVID-19 and RSV in 2025. Patients were identified based on hospital admission for acute respiratory infection and viral confirmation through nucleic acid detection.
analysis.main_results: In 2025, there were 8,749 hospitalisations of patients with influenza; 3,501 with COVID-19; and 5,105 with RSV reported at the 23 sentinel hospitals. Of patients hospitalised with influenza, 4,397 (50.3%) were children (1 year prior to admission. Of patients hospitalised with RSV, 1,551 (30.4%) were infants (< 1 year of age) and 3,723 (72.9%) were young children (< 5 years of age); 348 (6.8%) were Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander people; and 2,110 (41.3%) had chronic comorbidities.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Since 2022, influenza, RSV and COVID-19 have co-circulated. Assessment of vaccine effectiveness demonstrated protection against influenza hospitalisation and short-term protection against hospitalisation with COVID-19 in older people.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide insights into the epidemiology of RSV hospitalisations in Australia and highlight the importance of surveillance systems for understanding disease patterns and vaccine effectiveness.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on a sentinel surveillance system, which may not fully represent the entire population. The evidence is strong as it is derived from a well-established system with detailed demographic and clinical data.

analysis.summary_en: This study reports on the epidemiology of hospitalisations with laboratory-confirmed influenza, COVID-19, and RSV in 2025 using the FluCAN and PAEDS sentinel surveillance systems in Australia. It highlights the co-circulation of these pathogens since 2022 and provides demographic and clinical data on RSV cases, including the proportion of infants and young children affected, as well as the presence of chronic comorbidities. The study also notes the effectiveness of vaccines against influenza and short-term protection against COVID-19 in older populations. The findings underscore the importance of surveillance for understanding disease patterns and vaccine impact, though the study's reliance on a sentinel system may limit its generalisability.

title: Nirsevimab for RSV Prevention in India: Economic Viability and Implementation Pathways for National Introduction: A Review

analysis.scope_and_question: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) causes substantial morbidity and mortality in Indian infants, with an estimated 800,000–1.2 million annual hospitalizations. To evaluate the economic viability of Nirsevimab introduction in India and propose evidence-based implementation pathways aligned with national epidemiology and health system capacity.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A structured review of RSV disease burden, Nirsevimab clinical efficacy, and economic evidence was undertaken. An India-specific cohort decision-analytic model was constructed using WHO-recommended cost-effectiveness thresholds. Deterministic and probabilistic sensitivity analyses were performed, and phased implementation pathways were developed, incorporating supply considerations, program readiness, and integration with existing immunization platforms.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Economic modeling indicates an economically justifiable price of approximately ₹6,300 per dose. At ₹4,000 per dose, national introduction could prevent approximately 640,000 hospitalizations and 6,800 deaths annually while remaining highly cost-effective. Sensitivity analyses demonstrate robustness across plausible epidemiologic and pricing scenarios.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: At current market prices (₹40,000–₹80,000 per dose), universal Nirsevimab would consume 9–17% of India’s public health expenditure while exceeding accepted cost-effectiveness thresholds.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Nirsevimab can become a cost-effective RSV prevention strategy in India if differential pricing reduces per-dose cost to ₹4,000–₹6,000. A phased introduction prioritizing high-burden regions and high-risk infants offers a pragmatic pathway for national adoption.

analysis.summary_en: This review evaluates the economic viability and implementation pathways for introducing Nirsevimab, a monoclonal antibody, as an RSV prevention strategy in India. RSV causes significant morbidity and mortality in Indian infants, with an estimated 800,000–1.2 million annual hospitalizations. Economic modeling suggests that Nirsevimab could be cost-effective if the per-dose price is reduced to ₹4,000–₹6,000, potentially preventing 640,000 hospitalizations and 6,800 deaths annually. Sensitivity analyses show robustness across various scenarios, and a phased introduction targeting high-burden regions and high-risk infants is proposed as a practical approach. However, at current market prices, universal Nirsevimab introduction would be cost-prohibitive for India’s public health system.

title: Punicalin targets RSV glycoprotein and fusion protein at non-overlapping sites to prevent viral escape.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) causes substantial respiratory disease, while treatment is limited by drug resistance. The study aimed to identify potential new therapeutic agents that could overcome these limitations.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study evaluated the antiviral activity of punicalin (PUN) against RSV-A and RSV-B strains, including a clinical isolate, and tested its efficacy against strains resistant to existing drugs such as ziresovir, ribavirin, nirsevimab, and palivizumab.
analysis.methods: Molecular docking of a 3,880-compound natural-product library was used to identify punicalin as a dual-target RSV entry inhibitor. Mechanistic analyses were conducted to determine the interaction sites of PUN with the RSV glycoprotein and fusion protein.
analysis.main_results: After 20 passages under PUN selection, the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC 50 ) increases 3.88-fold, remaining below the predefined >10-fold resistance threshold. PUN interacts with the G protein cystine-noose region involving N178, N179, and W183 to inhibit attachment and with an F protein region involving V243, T245, and P246 to stabilize prefusion F and inhibit membrane fusion.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that punicalin targets RSV at non-overlapping sites from known resistance hotspots, which may reduce the likelihood of viral escape. This dual-target mechanism represents a novel approach to RSV inhibition.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results provide insights into the development of new antiviral strategies for RSV, potentially improving treatment options and reducing the risk of drug resistance in clinical settings.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to in vitro and in vivo experiments with RSV strains, and the evidence is based on molecular docking and mechanistic analyses. The confidence in these findings is moderate due to the lack of long-term clinical trials.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates punicalin as a dual-target inhibitor of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) entry. It identifies punicalin's interaction with the G and F proteins of RSV-A and RSV-B strains, including a clinical isolate, and demonstrates its effectiveness against drug-resistant variants. The findings suggest that punicalin's binding sites do not overlap known resistance hotspots, potentially reducing the risk of viral escape. In RSV-infected mice, nebulized punicalin reduces viral loads and pathology. The study's results highlight punicalin's potential as a new therapeutic agent for RSV, but the evidence is limited to in vitro and in vivo experiments, and further clinical validation is needed. The confidence in these findings is moderate due to the absence of long-term clinical trials.

title: Qualification of ELISA and PRNT methodologies to measure RSV humoral immunity using human clinical samples.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) represents a substantial public health burden worldwide, causing lower respiratory infections primarily in children under 5 and adults over 65.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study describes the methodologies and clinical qualification of two correlated RSV assays, an Enzyme Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) and a Plaque Reduction Neutralization Test (PRNT).
analysis.methods: We demonstrate each assay is precise, linear, and translational.
analysis.main_results: Clinically qualified endpoint assays are a crucial tool in these efforts, giving researchers insight into the magnitude, composition, and neutralization efficacies of the humoral immune response to RSV antigens.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: However, this protection is incomplete, highlighting the importance of continued research and development towards novel and improved therapeutics.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Publicly available controls increase reproducibility and transferability to other laboratories.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report design limitations, bias, confounding, sample size, controls, generalisability, or a justified high/moderate/low assessment.

analysis.summary_en: This study focuses on the qualification of ELISA and PRNT methodologies to measure RSV humoral immunity using human clinical samples. The research highlights the public health burden of RSV, particularly in vulnerable populations, and emphasizes the need for improved therapeutics. The study describes the development and validation of two assays, demonstrating their precision, linearity, and translational potential. These assays provide critical insights into the immune response to RSV antigens, which is essential for vaccine and monoclonal antibody development. The findings underscore the importance of standardized, reproducible methods in RSV research. Publicly available controls are noted to enhance the reproducibility and transferability of these assays across laboratories. The evidence is limited to abstract-level information, and the study does not provide detailed limitations or a comprehensive assessment of evidence strength.

title: Social disparities and the COVID-19, influenza, and RSV 'tripledemic' in Ontario, Canada: A population-based study.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to examine inequalities in hospitalization rates for respiratory viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus, during the 'tripledemic' period in Ontario, Canada, based on factors such as material deprivation, ethno-racial diversity, rurality, and sex.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was a population-based analysis conducted in Ontario, Canada, during the period from July 2020 to June 2023, comparing hospitalization rates across different neighbourhoods and demographic groups.
analysis.methods: Weekly hospitalization rates were calculated as the number of hospitalizations per 10 000 people, and local regression models were used to assess differences in peak hospitalization rates between subgroups, with statistical significance determined by the overlap of 95% confidence intervals.
analysis.main_results: More materially deprived neighbourhoods had up to a 2.5-times increase in peak weekly hospitalization rates compared to less deprived ones. Peak hospitalization rates were up to 2.3-times higher among more diverse neighbourhoods. Some age groups showed up to 2.8-times higher rates among urban residents. Younger males had up to 1.3-times higher rates than younger females, while older females had up to 1.6-times higher rates than older males.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings highlight the role of social determinants in shaping hospitalization rates for respiratory syncytial virus, offering new insights into how these factors contribute to health disparities during respiratory virus outbreaks.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results suggest that public health policies should account for neighbourhood-level material deprivation, ethno-racial diversity, rurality, and sex to effectively reduce the burden of respiratory syncytial virus.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on abstract-only data, which may limit the depth of analysis. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the reliance on observational trends rather than direct causal measures.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated social disparities in hospitalization rates for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in Ontario, Canada, during the 'tripledemic' period. It found that more materially deprived neighbourhoods had up to 2.5-times higher peak weekly hospitalization rates compared to less deprived ones. Additionally, more diverse neighbourhoods showed up to 2.3-times higher rates, and some age groups had up to 2.8-times higher rates among urban residents. Younger males had up to 1.3-times higher rates than younger females, while older females had up to 1.6-times higher rates than older males. The study emphasizes the importance of considering social determinants in public health policies to address RSV-related health disparities. However, the evidence is based on abstract-only data, which may limit the depth of analysis and the strength of the findings.

analysis.methods: The study used a cohort design to assess the effectiveness of reimmunization with a second nirsevimab dose against RSV hospitalization, employing observational data from the second season.
analysis.main_results: The results indicated a moderate effectiveness of reimmunization with a second nirsevimab dose against RSV hospitalization during the second season, with an estimated effectiveness of 42% (95% confidence interval: −25% to 73%).

title: Distinct mechanisms of neutralization by antibodies targeting a conserved pneumovirus F epitope

analysis.research_question_and_background: Pneumoviruses cause seasonal outbreaks leading to hospitalizations of vulnerable populations such as infants and the elderly. Cross-neutralizing antibodies targeting viral fusion have been isolated from infected individuals, but their elicitation and mechanisms of action remain understudied.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Here, we describe two vaccine-elicited antibody classes, LOR24 and LOR69, that bind an overlapping epitope, and identify the somatic mutations that endow their breadth and potency, respectively.
analysis.methods: Cryo-electron microscopy structures of both antibodies bound to the HRSV fusion (F) protein show binding modes distinct from each other and from the previously described cross-neutralizing antibody MPE8, yet they all use similar motifs for binding.
analysis.main_results: Complementary in vitro and electron microscopy experiments show that these antibodies either lock prefusion F as a trimer, arrest F in a monomeric or intermediate state, or promote the transition to the postfusion conformation.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: This work sheds light on mechanisms of pneumovirus neutralization and the elicitation of cross-neutralizing antibody responses.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: This study provides insights into the mechanisms of neutralization by antibodies targeting a conserved pneumovirus F epitope, which could inform the development of more effective vaccines and therapeutic strategies against RSV.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report limitations or evidence strength.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the mechanisms of neutralization by antibodies targeting a conserved epitope on the pneumovirus fusion (F) protein. The authors describe two vaccine-elicited antibody classes, LOR24 and LOR69, that bind to an overlapping epitope and identify the somatic mutations that contribute to their breadth and potency. Cryo-electron microscopy structures reveal distinct binding modes for these antibodies compared to each other and to the previously described cross-neutralizing antibody MPE8, yet they all utilize similar binding motifs. In vitro and electron microscopy experiments demonstrate that these antibodies can lock prefusion F as a trimer, arrest it in a monomeric or intermediate state, or promote its transition to the postfusion conformation. The findings highlight the mechanisms of pneumovirus neutralization and the elicitation of cross-neutralizing antibody responses, offering potential insights for vaccine and therapeutic development. The study is based on abstract-only evidence, and no limitations or evidence strength are explicitly reported.

title: Regional inequality in infant RSV morbidity and mortality burden in the era of expanded RSV passive immunisation: a global projection modelling study

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess regional inequality in infant RSV disease burden with and without the implementation of novel prophylactic products, addressing the disproportionate burden in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study re-analysed global RSV disease burden data in infants by WHO regions and World Bank Income Classification for 2019, using generalised linear mixed-effects models, and projected the impact of novel RSV prophylactic products by June 2025.
analysis.methods: Generalised linear mixed-effects models were used to re-analyse the previous global RSV disease burden dataset in infants, and a static deterministic model was developed to project the impact of novel RSV prophylactic products under two scenarios: no-implementation and June-2025 product use.
analysis.main_results: At baseline, the African Region had the highest incidence and mortality rates of RSV-associated ALRI and deaths, while the Eastern Mediterranean Region had the highest hospital admission rate. The implementation of novel prophylactic products was projected to avert 91,000 RSV-associated ALRI hospital admissions and 300 RSV-attributable deaths annually, with 90% of averted admissions and over 70% of averted deaths occurring in high-income countries.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study found that the current implementation of novel RSV prophylactic products is projected to yield only modest reductions in the global infant RSV disease burden, potentially exacerbating existing inequalities in RSV mortality burden.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings underscore the urgent need for targeted strategies to accelerate the introduction and scale-up of infant RSV immunisation programmes in LMICs, particularly the African Region, to reduce regional inequality in RSV disease burden.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the reliance on static deterministic models and the assumption of consistent implementation rates across countries, which may not accurately reflect real-world scenarios. The evidence strength is moderate.

analysis.summary_en: This study assessed regional inequality in infant RSV disease burden in LMICs and found that the current implementation of novel prophylactic products is projected to yield only modest reductions, potentially exacerbating existing inequalities.
